quote: Whoever saves a single life, it is as if he had saved the whole world.
content: The source is the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 4:5, and its context matters. The line is part of the warning given to witnesses in capital cases. Adam was created alone, it says, to teach that whoever destroys a single life is as though he destroyed a whole world, and whoever sustains one is as though he sustained a whole world. The point is the gravity of taking a single life by false testimony, the infinite worth of each person. That is closer to the non-aggregative intuition this essay argues against than to a "warm glow." Many manuscripts also read "a single soul of Israel," a variant that has itself been much discussed.

quote: I also hold that two human lives are twice as unimaginably valuable.
content: Whether numbers count, and how, is one of the central disputes of normative ethics, and the essay settles it by declaration. Taurek ("Should the Numbers Count?", Philosophy & Public Affairs, 1977; no DOI) argued that there is no impersonal sense in which two deaths are worse than one. Contractualists let numbers count only by breaking ties, not by summing (Scanlon, What We Owe to Each Other, 1998; book, no DOI). The rhetoric also undercuts itself. If one life has "unimaginably" high, unbounded value, "twice" adds nothing; if its value is finite, it isn't unimaginable.

quote: Whoever knowingly chooses to save one life, when they could have saved two—to say nothing of a thousand lives, or a world—they have damned themselves as thoroughly as any murderer.
content: Equating a failure to maximize with murder denies the distinction between doing and allowing, which most people and most moral theories accept. It also has consequences the book rejects elsewhere. By this standard nearly everyone who spends money on anything but the most effective charity is as guilty as a murderer, which is the demandingness objection in its sharpest form. And "Ends Don't Justify Means" later tells humans to keep deontological prohibitions even when breaking them would save more lives. On this essay's standard, that would make them murderers too.

quote: since cliché methods that instantly leap to mind don’t work or are counterproductive
content: The most clichéd method of all, giving poor people money, turned out to work well. Unconditional cash transfers in Kenya produced large gains in consumption and assets, with substantial positive spillovers to local economies and little inflation (Egger et al. 2022). Cash has become the benchmark other aid is measured against. Some clichés fail, but the evidence on aid doesn't show that intuitive methods generally "don't work or are counterproductive."
